<reason>Side A won by demonstrating that capping international recruitment builds zero additional housing while severing the cross-subsidy revenue that funds local bursaries and new construction. A's "secured bed precondition" alternative directly tied enrollment to physical capacity without scapegoating international students or starving university finances. While Side B effectively argued for binding capacity limits and a duty to local communities, A's argument that the cap treats a symptom (demand) while ignoring the disease (supply-side zoning failures), combined with the exposure of the arbitrary "severe" trigger and the contradiction in B's housing-market claims, gave A the stronger path to victory. Side B also incurred execution costs from clipped turns in the opening and Rebuttal 2.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Side A's Pressure Question Q1 was decisive: it forced Side B to resolve the contradiction between claiming international students occupy purpose-built housing (absorbing demand) and simultaneously bid up family rentals (displacing locals). B's concession that students "overflow" into shared houses only after purpose-built beds fill weakened the direct displacement mechanism and revealed the cap's blunt imprecision.</best_rebuttal>
